channel.description: Debezium is an open source distributed platform for change data capture. Start it up, point it at your databases, and your apps can start responding to all of the inserts, updates, and deletes that other apps commit to your databases. Debezium is durable and fast, so your apps can respond quickly and never miss an event, even when things go wrong.

item.title: Debezium CLI: A Unified Command-Line Interface for CDC Pipeline Lifecycle Management
item.dc:creator: Binayak Das
item.description:
Change Data Capture (CDC) has established itself as the gold standard for real-time data streaming, cache invalidation, outbox pattern implementations, and microservice data synchronizations. For years, the Debezium project has empowered engineers worldwide to stream row-level database changes reliably into Apache Kafka, Apache Pulsar, Redis, and dozens of downstream cloud messaging platforms.

However, operating CDC pipelines traditionally came with operational friction. Developers had to hand-craft nested JSON connector configurations, deploy them via raw curl commands to Kafka Connect REST endpoints, navigate differing configuration dialects for standalone Debezium Server distributions, or manage complex Kubernetes manifests manually. With the introduction of the Debezium Platform, the ecosystem gained a robust control plane, but developers and platform engineers still needed a fast, intuitive, unified tool right in their terminal.

As part of Google Summer of Code (GSoC) 2026, we designed and built the Debezium CLI (debezium-jbang): a modern, zero-dependency command-line interface that covers the entire lifecycle of Debezium pipelines, from local scaffolding and daemonless container image assembly to real-time schema discovery and remote platform orchestration.

In this post, we explore the motivation, architecture, key capabilities, and hands-on workflows powered by the new Debezium CLI.

Why a Unified CLI?

The primary design principle behind Debezium CLI is developer velocity without infrastructure overhead. Whether an engineer is prototyping a new pipeline locally on their laptop or an SRE is auditing pipelines across multiple Kubernetes clusters, the CLI delivers:

  • Zero-Friction Installation: Powered by JBang, the CLI requires no manual Java compilation, package manager friction, or Maven installation. It runs everywhere Java or JBang is present, and supports instant execution via the Debezium catalog: jbang debezium@debezium.

  • Daemonless Distribution and Container Builds: Build custom Debezium Server distribution archives and layered OCI container images without needing a local Maven runtime or a running Docker daemon.

  • Unified Control Plane: Seamlessly manage connectors, transformations, destinations, and pipelines against Debezium Platform instances across development, staging, and production environments.

  • Live Discovery & Diagnostics: Discover database catalogs, validate connection credentials against live source databases, inspect schema collections, and stream runtime pipeline logs directly in the terminal.

Capabilities Overview

Under the hood, the Debezium CLI is built on Picocli and is organized into two primary, complementary subsystems:

Subsystem Commands Core Responsibilities

Build Subsystem

init, validate, build, push

Scaffolds dbz.yaml, performs static analysis, resolves Maven dependencies dynamically via Eclipse Aether, and builds layered OCI images via Google Jib Core without Docker.

Platform Subsystem

switch, config, catalog, source, destination, connection, transform, pipeline

Interfaces with the Debezium Platform REST API, providing multi-environment profiles, schema exploration, runtime health checks, and signal emission.

Getting Started

Getting started with the Debezium CLI takes less than thirty seconds.

Prerequisites

The Debezium CLI is distributed via JBang. If you don’t have JBang installed yet, you can install it on your system with a single command:

# macOS / Linux $ curl -Ls https://sh.jbang.dev | bash -s - app setup # Windows (PowerShell) $ iex "& { $(iwr -useb https://ps.jbang.dev) } app setup"

You can also use your preferred package manager (such as brew install jbangdev/tap/jbang or sdk install jbang). For other platforms and installation methods, see the official JBang installation guide.

Installation

With JBang installed, you can install the Debezium CLI globally from the official {prodname} catalog:

$ jbang app install debezium@debezium $ debezium --version

Alternatively, you can run commands directly on the fly without permanent installation:

$ jbang debezium@debezium --help

Once installed, explore all available commands using debezium --help.

Phase 1: Local Development & The Build Subsystem

The Build subsystem empowers developers to go from zero to a fully packaged, deployable Debezium Server container image in seconds, all governed by a declarative project descriptor: dbz.yaml.

1. Scaffolding a Project (init)

To scaffold a new CDC project, simply run debezium init specifying your source database and target sink:

$ debezium init --source postgres --sink kafka

This creates a templated dbz.yaml file pre-configured for your chosen source and sink:

# Debezium Server Configuration version: "1.0" debezium: version: "3.7.0.Alpha2" source: connector: "postgres" config: database.hostname: "${DBZ_DB_HOST:-localhost}" database.port: "${DBZ_DB_PORT:-5432}" database.user: "${DBZ_DB_USER}" database.password: "${DBZ_DB_PASS}" database.dbname: "${DBZ_DB_NAME:-inventory}" topic.prefix: "inventory" sink: type: "kafka" config: bootstrap.servers: "${DBZ_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP:-localhost:9092}" build: target: "tar" image: name: "debezium-server" registry: "ghcr.io/my-org" tag: "latest"

2. Static Analysis & Environment Validation (validate)

Before triggering any build, debezium validate verifies syntax, checks required fields, and audits referenced environment variables:

$ export DBZ_DB_USER=postgres $ export DBZ_DB_PASS=secretpassword $ debezium validate Project descriptor dbz.yaml is valid!

If a mandatory variable is missing, the validator alerts you before any resource is consumed.

3. Daemonless OCI Image Assembly (build)

Traditionally, building a custom Debezium Server container required writing a multi-stage Dockerfile, running a local Docker daemon, and downloading multi-gigabyte Maven dependency trees.

The Debezium CLI solves this using the Google Jib Core API and dynamic Eclipse Aether (Maven Resolver):

$ debezium build --image
Resolving dependencies for Debezium Server 3.7.0.Alpha2 (postgres -> kafka)... Resolved 48 artifacts (184 MB) in 4.2s. Assembling layered OCI image target/debezium-server.tar... [Layer 1/3] Base runtime: eclipse-temurin:21-jre-jammy [Layer 2/3] Debezium Server runtime libraries [Layer 3/3] User configurations and startup scripts Built OCI image archive: target/debezium-server.tar (image: debezium-server:postgres-kafka-latest)

No Docker daemon required! The build runs inside CI runners, unprivileged Kubernetes pods, or developer laptops with equal fidelity.

4. Pushing to Container Registries (push)

Once the image tarball is assembled, debezium push publishes it directly to your target container registry:

# Push to Docker Hub or GitHub Container Registry: $ debezium push --registry ghcr.io/my-org # Or push to a local/insecure development registry: $ debezium push --registry localhost:5001 --allow-insecure-registries
Pushing debezium-server:postgres-kafka-latest -> localhost:5001... No credentials found — attempting anonymous push... Pushed: localhost:5001/debezium-server:postgres-kafka-latest Pull with: docker pull localhost:5001/debezium-server:postgres-kafka-latest

You can see the push workflow in action below:

Phase 2: Remote Orchestration & The Platform Subsystem

While the Build subsystem handles standalone packaging, modern architectures frequently rely on the Debezium Platform for centralized orchestration, dynamic reconfigurations, and centralized telemetry. The Debezium CLI provides native integration with the Platform API.

1. Multi-Environment Switching (config & switch)

Switching between development, testing, and production clusters is instant:

# Register and switch environments $ debezium config set --env=dev platform-url http://localhost:8080 $ debezium config set --env=staging platform-url https://platform.staging.internal:8080 $ debezium switch dev Switched to environment: dev $ debezium config get NAME URL ACTIVE ---- --- ------ dev http://localhost:8080 * staging https://platform.staging.internal:8080 Effective platform URL: http://localhost:8080

2. Discovering Connector Capabilities (catalog)

No need to browse documentation to find connector configuration properties. The CLI queries the live platform catalog directly:

$ debezium catalog list TYPE CLASS ------ -------------------------------------------------- source io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector source io.debezium.connector.mysql.MySqlConnector $ debezium catalog get source io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector
Name: Debezium PostgreSQL Connector Type: source-connector Version: 3.7.0-SNAPSHOT Description: Captures row-level changes from a PostgreSQL database in near real-time. NAME TYPE REQUIRED DEFAULT DESCRIPTION ----------------- ------ -------- ------- ----------- database.hostname string true Resolvable hostname or IP address. database.port number false 5432 Port of the database server. database.user string true Name of the database user.

JSON output is also supported via --format=json, making programmatic integration with CI/CD pipelines trivial.

3. Live Connection Validation & Database Discovery (connection)

Before creating a pipeline, the CLI lets you test your database credentials against the live network and inspect database schemas directly:

# Validate database connection parameters: $ debezium connection validate -f connection.yaml Connection is valid. # Discover schemas and tables in the target database: $ debezium connection collections 1 public public.customers public.orders public.order_lines public.products

4. Managing Pipelines & Sending Signals (pipeline)

Once sources and destinations are registered, creating and orchestrating pipelines takes a single command:

$ debezium pipeline create -f pipeline.yaml Pipeline created with id: 1 $ debezium pipeline list ID NAME SOURCE DESTINATION LOG LEVEL --- ---- ------ ----------- --------- 1 customer-sync pg-source kafka-dest INFO

Need to trigger an ad-hoc incremental snapshot or pause ingestion for maintenance? Use the pipeline signal command:

# Trigger an incremental snapshot: $ debezium pipeline signal --type=execute-snapshot \ --data='{"data-collections": ["public.customers"]}' 1 Signal sent to pipeline 1. # Adjust logging verbosity or pause ingestion: $ debezium pipeline signal --type=pause 1 Signal sent to pipeline 1.

What’s Next

While the Debezium CLI already covers core build and orchestration workflows in Debezium 3.7, several enhancements are planned for future releases:

  • Interactive Terminal User Interface (TUI): A rich, dynamic terminal dashboard for monitoring pipeline health, throughput rates, and event latencies in real time.

  • Operator Integration: Tighter bidirectional integration with the Debezium Kubernetes Operator for managing Custom Resources (DebeziumServer, etc.) directly from the CLI.

  • Consumer Lag and Health Diagnostics: Advanced diagnostics (debezium doctor) to audit database permissions, verify network reachability, and monitor consumer group lag.

  • Expanded Connector and Sink Templates: Additional scaffolding presets for emerging sources and sinks across the Debezium ecosystem.

Acknowledgements & GSoC 2026 Reflection

The Debezium CLI was designed and implemented during Google Summer of Code 2026.

A heartfelt and special thank you to my mentors, Giovanni Panice and Mario Fiore Vitale, for their invaluable guidance, detailed architectural feedback, and supportive code reviews throughout the program. Working alongside the Debezium core team has been an extraordinary learning journey in building resilient, enterprise-grade developer tooling for the open-source data streaming ecosystem.

We encourage everyone in the Debezium community to try out the new CLI, share feedback in the #community-platform channel on Zulip, and contribute ideas for upcoming releases!

item.title: Native Support for Debezium in Apache Beam
item.dc:creator: Ilyas Ahsan
item.description:
Apache Beam has a built-in connector for Debezium called DebeziumIO. It lets you capture changes from your database and process them directly inside a Beam pipeline. You don’t need to run Apache Kafka or Kafka Connect.

In this post, we’ll build an example pipeline that streams changes from MySQL into Google BigQuery. The complete example is available in the debezium-examples repository.

item.title: Introducing PyDebeziumAI: Real-Time CDC for LangChain and LangGraph
item.dc:creator: Kodukulla Mohnish Mythreya
item.description:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a central pattern in AI application development. The idea is simple: rather than relying solely on an LLM’s pre-trained knowledge, you give it fresh context by retrieving relevant documents from a vector store at query time.

But there is a catch that most tutorials skip over entirely. Where does that vector data come from, and how do you keep it current?

Today, most teams answer that question with a cron job, a nightly batch reload, or a manual re-embedding script. That approach works until the database changes faster than the schedule runs, and your AI starts answering questions based on data that no longer exists or doesn’t reflect a new record committed five minutes ago.

This is the problem that PyDebeziumAI solves. It is an open-source Python library, developed as part of Google Summer of Code 2026 under the Debezium project, that wires Debezium’s Change Data Capture engine directly into LangChain and LangGraph pipelines, ensuring your vector store updates the moment the database does.

item.title: Concluding Debezium’s Google Summer of Code 2026 Program
item.dc:creator: Giovanni Panice
item.description:
The Google Summer of Code 2026 program has officially concluded for Debezium, and we are delighted to announce that all our contributors successfully passed their final evaluations! 🎉

Over the past few months, our contributors have worked closely with their mentors and the wider community to design, implement, test, and document new capabilities across the Debezium ecosystem.

Their work was not simply an academic exercise or a collection of experimental prototypes. These contributions address real use cases and are already valuable to the many companies and developers who rely on Debezium. The results are included in Debezium 3.7, which was recently released.

Before looking at what comes next, let’s take a moment to celebrate the contributors and the projects they delivered.

The Debezium Platform UI gives you a central place to design pipelines, configure sources, transforms, and destinations, and keep an eye on what is running. Over the last few preview releases, we have shipped improvements that make that work faster and clearer, with less need to leave the UI to look something up.

This post walks through four of those changes:

item.title: Debezium 3.7.0.CR1 Released
item.dc:creator: Chris Cranford
item.description:
With autumn officially underway, we’re pleased to announce Debezium 3.7.0.CR1, the first release candidate for the 3.7 series, focused on stability and polish ahead of the final release.

Among the highlights, PyDebeziumAI brings real-time change data capture to LangChain and LangGraph applications, the Oracle connector gains new tools for monitoring and troubleshooting long-running transactions, and MongoDB now keeps streaming from the preferred replica set member after a failover. This release also includes important reliability fixes for MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, and Oracle, along with numerous other improvements across the board.

Read on for the full details!

item.title: Debezium 3.6.3.Final Released
item.dc:creator: Chris Cranford
item.description:
We’re pleased to announce Debezium 3.6.3.Final, a maintenance release focused on stability and reliability improvements.

The Oracle connector receives the most attention in this release, with corrected savepoint partial rollback handling for tables with LOB columns, a fix for unbounded mining sessions with the log-count mining algorithm, and ORA-02002 now treated as a retriable error so the connector can recover from failovers. The MySQL and MariaDB connectors once again restart automatically after transient communication errors, while the SQL Server, Vitess, and Informix connectors pick up targeted fixes ranging from ambiguous column name errors to irregular heartbeat intervals. If you use the Oracle connector with an Ehcache or Infinispan buffer, be sure to review the breaking changes before upgrading.

Read on for the full details!

item.dc:creator: Chris Cranford
item.description:
As the leaves start to turn, we’re pleased to announce Debezium 3.7.0.Beta2, a release that delivers the first official release of the Milvus and SQLite source connectors and the Debezium CLI, alongside new capabilities across the platform, core library, and connectors.

Among the highlights, the Debezium Platform gains alerting, the reselect columns post processor gets a RocksDB-backed cache, a new embeddings transformation supports OpenAI models, and a rework of the JMX LastEvent metric rendering delivers improved snapshot throughput. Debezium Server adds TLS and mutual TLS support for the RabbitMQ Stream sink, and the JDBC sink can now map arrays to SingleStore JSON columns.

Read on for the full details!

item.title: Debezium 3.6.2.Final Released
item.dc:creator: Chris Cranford
item.description:
As summer winds down, we’re pleased to announce Debezium 3.6.2.Final, a maintenance release packed with correctness, performance, and security improvements across the entire connector family.

Among the highlights, incremental snapshots now work on PostgreSQL read-only replicas, and a fix to Debezium’s internal caching keeps long-running connectors from gradually losing throughput. On the security front, Debezium Server now masks passwords in its logs, and the PostgreSQL JDBC driver has been bumped to 42.7.13 to address CVE-2026-54291. Rounding things out are a healthy batch of DDL parser fixes for MySQL and Oracle, data-correctness fixes for incremental snapshots and heartbeat error handling, and improved PostgreSQL parallel snapshot consistency.

Read on for the full details!

item.title: Single Sign-On for the Debezium Platform
item.dc:creator: Philippe Camus
item.description:
Identity and Access Management is a highly anticipated feature for the Debezium Platform, slatted for Q4.

Until then, we can explore what is currently possible: Single Sign-on, OpenID Connect, and even brokering Entra ID. In this first post, I will walk you through putting a Debezium Platform deployment on Kubernetes behind a single sign-on (SSO) login with Keycloak as an Identity Provider.

The scenario throughout the blog series is Contoso Retail, a fictional company on the domain contoso.com, running the Platform on a Kubernetes cluster and wanting its own staff list to govern access to it. Contoso Retail uses Entra ID as its corporate directory.

item.description:
As summer continues, we’re excited to announce the release of Debezium 3.7.0.Beta1, bringing a broad set of improvements across connectors, Debezium Server, and the Platform UI.

Among the highlights, incremental snapshots now work on PostgreSQL read-only replicas, and Debezium Server gains a new Databricks ZeroBus Ingest sink for direct change event delivery to Unity Catalog-managed Delta tables. This release also includes performance and snapshot optimizations, new connector capabilities, and numerous bug fixes across the board.

Read on for the full details!

item.title: Debezium 3.7.0.Alpha2 Released
item.dc:creator: Chris Cranford
item.description:
We’re pleased to announce the release of Debezium 3.7.0.Alpha2, the second preview release in the 3.7 series, packed with new features and important changes across the platform.

This release introduces an incubating TiDB connector, adds retry and dead letter queue support for the JDBC sink, and improves Debezium Server with a proper readiness probe. On the Oracle side, the OpenLogReplicator client is now non-blocking and continuous mining for Oracle 12 has been removed. The Debezium Platform UI now surfaces pipeline failures directly, and several other connectors receive important fixes and improvements.

Let’s take a closer look at all these changes and more; read on for the full details!

item.title: Debezium 3.6.1.Final Released
item.dc:creator: Chris Cranford
item.description:
We’re pleased to announce the release of Debezium 3.6.1.Final, a maintenance release that delivers important data integrity and security improvements across multiple connectors.

This release fixes several issues that could affect change event accuracy, including correct parsing of BC-era dates in PostgreSQL, proper mapping of MySQL INTEGER UNSIGNED columns, and resolution of Oracle RowId corruption in change events. The JDBC sink connector also receives a fix for tsvector data handling, and credential leakage has been addressed in log output and configuration serialization.

Read on for the full details!

item.dc:creator: Chris Cranford
item.description:
As summer heats up, so does the pace of innovation in the Debezium community. We’re thrilled to announce Debezium 3.7.0.Alpha1, the first preview release of the 3.7 series, packed with new features and improvements.

Highlights include an incubating Ingres connector, a new ExtendedTimestamp type for high-precision timestamps, and expanded JDBC sink support with CockroachDB, SingleStore, and Starrocks dialects. The release also brings schema history memory optimization, Debezium Engine shutdown strategies, and numerous platform, connector, and performance improvements. Read on for the full details!

item.title: Running the Debezium Platform on AWS: PostgreSQL to Amazon Kinesis
item.dc:creator: Philippe Camus
item.description:
In his recent mid-year update, Mario highlighted the incredible work he and his team have done to make the Debezium Platform operational on Kubernetes. So let us take it somewhere concrete: Amazon Web Services.

This post stands the Platform up on a single-node k3s cluster on an EC2 instance and builds a real change-data-capture pipeline from Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL to Amazon Kinesis. The deployment itself is done through a couple of simple commands via a companion project that does the heavy lifting, so the focus is the AWS-specific friction that documentation is thin on: IAM for the Kinesis sink, Kinesis stream naming, RDS logical replication, and reading a change event back out of the stream to prove it all works.

item.title: No More Tuning: Oracle Log Mining Simplified in Debezium 3.6
item.dc:creator: Chris Cranford
item.description:
If you have ever deployed the Debezium Oracle connector in an environment with bursty workloads, you have probably spent more time than you would like tuning the log.mining.batch.size.*, log.mining.sleep.time.*, and log.mining.scn.gap.detection.* properties. Getting the balance right between peak and quiet periods was, frankly, a losing battle — what worked for your nightly ETL window would over-read during the day, and what worked during the day would fall hopelessly behind at night.

In Debezium 3.6, we replaced this entire mechanism. The connector now selects mining windows based on log file count rather than SCN ranges, controlled by a single new property: log.mining.log.count.min. This post explains why the old approach was so hard to tune, how the new approach works, and what you need to know to migrate.


Read more...

item.title: Building Kafka-Less Data Integration Pipelines with Debezium
item.dc:creator: Fiore Mario Vitale
item.description:
Debezium is often associated with Kafka, and while this was true in the project’s early days, it is no longer the case. We explained in detail, together with several other common misconceptions, in our recent article, "What Nobody Explains About Debezium in 2026 (But Should)".

In this article, we’ll build on that discussion by showing the recently added JDBC sink support in Debezium Server (DS) and the Debezium Management Platform (DMP), which opens up Kafka-less data replication and migration scenarios.
